en: All these AI models you may be interacting
with, no matter if it's in agents or in
software you may be building on top of these
large language models,
all these models come with benchmarks that
are typically released when the model is
released. So all these AI companies,
whenever they launch a new model version,
they typically publish a bunch of benchmark
results showing you how amazing the model
is.
And it's quite common that, of course, every
new model that is being released performs
very well in all those released benchmarks.
It's of course also worth noting though that
every company
publishes different benchmarks results, at
least to some degree. And the reason for
that of course is that the model may simply
not perform that well in all the benchmarks.
Either way, those benchmark results are to
be taken with a grain of salt.
They definitely do prove that the model
is quite good, but nowadays it's also quite
easy and common
to optimize models to perform well in
benchmarks. And therefore, whenever you see
benchmark numbers that are there to prove
how good and how intelligent a certain model
is,
you should keep in mind that the model
was most likely optimized to perform well in
those benchmarks, and the results you're
seeing in your day-to-day use therefore may
be worse. It's possible that it's a really
amazing model that performs well for you
too, but it's also possible that the tasks
you give to a model may not live up to what
you saw in those benchmarks.
